title: The barren spring as figure of the church, and Zacchaeus the chief tax collector
english: So the water at the spring ran to no purpose. The neighbors often stood by and groaned, not because they had no water, but because the sight of those useless waters dragged them into thirst. They could not cure the suffering of their thirst, and in their misery they cried out to the spring: “Why do you flow to no purpose, O spring? It would be better for you not to appear at all, but to flow among mountains and sands and deserts, where you would not have so many witnesses to your evil.”

Why was the water undrinkable? Because it killed the bodies of those who drank it. If a man drank from it, he did not become a father; nor did a woman become a mother, for she lost the grace of motherhood. And not only this: the earth that received the stream refused its usual yield of grain, and the shady graces of the palm trees stripped off their garment of leaves. To say it all at once, everything became desolate, as if it had unjustly fallen in with that stream.

Such was the spring that encircled Jericho in ancient times, until the prophet Elisha came, took salt, threw it into the spring, and made the waters alive. For this is what the Lord says: “I heal these waters” (2 Kings 2:21). This is what he says who always speaks and brings his word to deed: “Let there no longer be from you one barren and sterile.” He spoke, and the water was changed: wombs were in labor, the earth put forth grain, the grape clusters bloomed again, and the olive tree displayed its own grace. And the neighbors were reconciled to the spring they knew. Once they had warred against it and been warred against by it; later they longed for it and lived near it.

What does the riddle of the spring mean? It is necessary to say. This spring, flowing abundantly but pouring out a useless and barren stream in ancient times, preserves the account of the church. For before Christ, it was so impious that a man drinking from the spring of that stream lost the very fact of being human, denying the nature of his rational soul through entanglement with idols. And a woman did not become a mother of virtues, nor did she give birth to shoots of self-control or gush the white milk of piety. But while she was in this condition, the Lord came, threw in the apostles as salt, seasoned her, and made her drinkable. And that the apostles were salt, hear Christ saying to them: “You are the salt of the earth” (Matthew 5:13). And that the sterile and barren one became fruitful by receiving the apostolic salt, the prophet says: “Rejoice, O barren one who does not bear; break forth and shout, you who are not in labor; for the children of the desolate one are more than those of her who has a husband” (Isaiah 54:1).

So Jesus came to Jericho. The spring came to those nourished by the spring; the mighty grace came to the much-wooded and well-watered city. And behold, a man named Zacchaeus, and he was a chief tax collector. The evil was double: he pursued an unjust trade and ruled over those who pursued it badly. He not only sinned himself but also received the evils of others. He cut a strange road of injustice, fortifying the highways against travelers. He did not imitate robbers by ambushing those passing by, nor did he wait for travelers out of zeal for hospitality. Instead, holding injustice as a law, he taxed the labors of foreigners, imitating the merciless gluttony of drones. For just as drones harvest the labor of bees without taking part in the toil, so tax collectors plunder the labors of strangers, the travelers, idling in leisure and sitting at the crossroads. A man sailed the sea, fought the waves, battled the winds, cut through the long and ungovernable deep, and Zacchaeus took away his profit with a tax.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
orientation: Amphilochius is explaining how the deadly spring of Jericho, healed by Elisha's salt, prefigures the church healed by Christ through the apostles, and he now turns to Zacchaeus as a chief tax collector in Jericho.

title: Zacchaeus climbs the sycamore to test whether Jesus knows hearts
english: A shepherd lived with drought and burning heat, with rain and snow and frost. His shelter was the ledges of the rocks, his food cheese and milk, his clothing the unworked skins of his sheep. Yet this rustic, this poor man, this companion of the mountains, fell into Zacchaeus's hands, being tithed of his flocks, being robbed lawfully, being destroyed without a sword. For a man struck by iron receives a wound that flows easily and departs, escaping the harshness of his suffering through numbness. But a man unwillingly shot by poverty's arrow has pain as his death, and he has died, not consumed all at once, but dying always, little by little. And to put it briefly: as fortresses hard to capture are dreaded by soldiers, and underwater rocks by pilots, and hidden ambushes by those at war, so Zacchaeus was to be fled by merchants and travelers, by cowherds and shepherds.

But this man, so maddened over the irrational collection of money, was seeking to see Jesus and could not. For both the smallness of his stature and the heaviness of his injustice held him back. So now, healing the lowliness of his stature by the device of his understanding, he ran ahead and climbed up into a sycamore, and he hides himself under the dense cover of the leaves, thinking he sees and is not seen, supposing he can escape the notice of the one who knows all things. This is exactly what the woman with the flow of blood also ventured, thinking she could steal from Jesus, the one who gladly lets such things be stolen from him. But she at least came near and touched the hem of his garment; this man, being far off, took hold of Christ by faith. So he goes up onto the tree, healing the evils of Adam. For Adam was led astray by the tree while fleeing God, but this man is saved from the tree while longing to see God.

For hearing that Jesus works many astonishing wonders, that he heals souls as well as bodies, taking away the sins of souls and granting freedom from suffering to bodies, Zacchaeus longed to see the one who pardons all things to all people. He reasoned within himself:

"Who then is this Jesus, who cleanses lepers, who heals the blind, who forgives sins to those who ask? What is his appearance, what is his form? Does he know all things? Does he test the minds even of those who are absent? Or does he examine only the thoughts of those who are present? Does he, as God, trace out the thoughts of each person's heart? How then can I learn these things? What teacher shall I take for them? What teacher? Experience, the teacher of all things. I have climbed the tree and hide myself under the dense cover of the leaves. I escape notice and I learn whether I can be saved. If he knows the movement of my soul, I know that he wipes away the sin of my soul. This one thing then I will learn: that he knows the hidden things of my thoughts. If, pressed by the crowd, he sees me hiding, and not only sees me but also uncovers the longing of my soul, I choose to throw away everything and find the one. I want to imitate Matthew. For he too was a tax collector, as I am. But Matthew did not run to him of his own accord; rather, he was called and obeyed. Perhaps, seeing him and thinking him one of the travelers, he hollowed his hands and spread wide his deep pocket, carried along by habit toward the taking, and wanting to collect taxes from Christ, he was collected from in return by him, not in appearance only, but giving his whole self over. For as soon as he heard, 'Come, follow me,' he outran the call with his eagerness, outrunning with swifter speed the one who drew him. If then he calls tax collectors, and not only calls them but also makes them righteous, the swarm of my previous evils does not harm me. For if Elisha threw salt into the nourishing spring and made its barrenness fruitful, surely this man also, seasoning my soul with grace as with salt, stirs up in me the fruit-bearing of virtue."

While he was pondering these things, Jesus came to the place. Looking up, he says to him: "Zacchaeus, hurry and come down. You climbed the tree as a tax collector; come down from the tree as a lover of God. Come down from the tree to the earth, so that through the cross you may go up to heaven. You went up a tree hiding from human beings; you are going up through the cross, granting a gift to angels."
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
orientation: Amphilochius is imagining Zacchaeus's interior reasoning as he climbs the sycamore to see Jesus, after describing how Zacchaeus exploited shepherds and travelers.

title: Christ's lodging with Zacchaeus defended against the murmurers
english: “Hurry and come down,” he says, “for today I must stay in your house” (Luke 19:5). O grace beyond telling! O love for humanity beyond speech! For wherever Jesus is received as a guest, everything is changed for the better.

“Zacchaeus,” he says, “hurry and come down, for today I must stay in your house.” What can I say? The tax collector’s house has become paradise. For what I see in the thief I see also in Zacchaeus. He said to the thief, “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43), and taking him from the tree he brought him into paradise. He said to Zacchaeus, “Today I must stay in your house,” and taking him he entered, and by entering he made his house a paradise before paradise itself.
And Zacchaeus hurried down and ran ahead and received him joyfully. And Jesus called him a son of Abraham.
But the murmurers, who were always ready to murmur, said among themselves, “He has gone in to lodge with a sinful man” (Luke 19:7).

O workers of contempt and cultivators of idleness! What are you—righteous or sinners? Are you not more wicked than all people? How then did Jesus dwell among you? How was he born among you, raised among you, grow to manhood among you, drink among you, eat among you? Why do you overlook your own wounds and hunt out your neighbor’s stumbles?

And besides, why do you call Christ a sinner at one time and a righteous man at another? For when he healed the man born blind, you called him a sinner, saying, “Give glory to God; we know that this man is a sinner, because he breaks the Sabbath” (John 9:24). Now, when he has gone under the roof of a tax collector, you slander him as one who unworthily eats with sinners, as if he were a righteous man. We played the flute for you and you did not dance; we sang a dirge for you and you did not beat your breasts (Matthew 11:17). For if he heals a blind man, you call him a sinner; and if he eats with sinners, you slander him as one unworthily eating with sinners.

What then? Should he not heal a blind man on the Sabbath, so that he may not be thought a sinner? Should he not eat with tax collectors, so that he may not be suspected of being righteous? Why do you accuse him for going in to lodge with a sinful man? And where should the light have been placed except in the darkness? For the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it (John 1:5). Where should the physician have gone? Let him run to the sick! For those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are ill (Matthew 9:12). Where should the Lamb of God have appeared? Was it not to tax collectors and sinners, so that taking up their burden he might set them free? You revile him in vain. For what was spoken has been fulfilled in you: prostitutes and tax collectors go before you into the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 21:31), you Pharisees.

Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord, “Look, half of my possessions I give to the poor, and if I have extorted anything from anyone, I repay it fourfold” (Luke 19:8). For I no longer endure wronging the poor, having received you, the shelter of the poor, into my house. I no longer tremble over the gathering of money, having found true wealth. I no longer stand at the gates watching travelers in human form. I have received amnesty for my former sins. Though rich, he remained in poverty. Foxes have holes and the birds of the air have nests, but you have nowhere to lay your head (Matthew 8:20). Let courts and porches go, the grand works of builders, bright and splendid houses. For in place of all these I seek your inexhaustible wealth hidden in poverty.

But since I cannot describe at greater length the wealth of Zacchaeus’s soul, let us leave the word to the Father who is rich in virtues. For it is fitting that the hospitable one describe the virtues of the hospitable one, for his praise, for your strengthening, for the crown of the church, and for the honor of Christ, to whom be glory and power forever and ever. Amen.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
orientation: Amphilochius is closing his homily on Zacchaeus, defending Christ's lodging with the tax collector against critics and praising Zacchaeus's restitution.
